case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court vacated an abuse-and-neglect adjudication because the family court failed to decide the truth or falsity of the petition's allegations under KRS 620.100(3), relied on evidence outside the record, and used the DNA hearing to resolve custody.
key_cases.relevance: This is the working Kentucky statement of the adjudication standard: the complainant bears the burden and must prove each allegation by a preponderance.
key_cases.quote: The family court did not follow the statutory requirement that it determine the truth or falsity of the allegations in the complaint

key_cases.case_name: Commonwealth, Cabinet for Health & Family Services ex rel. M.H. v. R.H.
key_cases.holding: The court held that issue preclusion did not bar the Cabinet from introducing evidence identifying a parent as the perpetrator of prior sexual abuse of the child's seven siblings, because the earlier court had not actually decided the perpetrator's identity and that identity is not material to a finding that a parent created a risk of sexual abuse; it vacated the dismissal and ordered an expedited adjudication.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a risk-of-harm finding for one child may rest on adjudicated abuse of that child's siblings, a core substantiation theory in Kentucky.
key_cases.quote: The identity of the perpetrator of the abuse is not material to that finding.

key_cases.case_name: V.S. v. Commonwealth, Cabinet for Health & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court vacated the termination of an absent mother's parental rights because a fifteen-minute hearing with one conclusory social-worker witness was not clear and convincing evidence; the parent's failure to appear did not shift the Cabinet's burden, and the Cabinet never showed the home's condition was attributable to something other than poverty.
key_cases.relevance: It requires concrete evidentiary support - not a caseworker's conclusion - for findings of educational and medical neglect.
key_cases.quote: we observe that the Cabinet did not show that V.S.'s allegedly substandard home was due to factors other than poverty alone, as required by KRS 625.090(2)(g)

key_cases.case_name: D.G.R. v. Commonwealth, Cabinet for Health & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The Court reinstated a trial court's refusal to terminate parental rights, holding that only a decision to terminate must rest on clear and convincing evidence, that parents may defeat termination by showing by a preponderance that the child will not be abused in the future, and that the KRS 625.090(3) best-interest factors are to be considered rather than treated as a checklist.
key_cases.relevance: The Court explained that the abused-or-neglected finding underlying termination must itself be made by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: the Cabinet must prove the necessary statutory allegations by clear and convincing evidence in order for the trial court to terminate parental rights

key_cases.case_name: C.R.G. v. Cabinet for Health & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court declined to treat appointed counsel's no-merit briefs as Anders briefs because no motions to withdraw accompanied them, independently reviewed the record, and affirmed the termination as supported by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This states the deference Kentucky appellate courts give to a trial court's abuse-or-neglect categorization.
key_cases.quote: The trial court has broad discretion in determining whether a child fits within the abused or neglected category and whether the abuse or neglect warrants termination
